newsitem.title: BRAZIL: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE HAS POLE IN BRAZIL.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE HAS POLE IN BRAZIL.

text.p: Canadian Jacques Villeneuve earned pole position for Sunday's Brazilian Grand Prix by dominating Saturday's qualifying at the Interlagos track in Sao Paulo.
The 25-year-old Williams driver went fastest on his opening run after only eight minutes of the one- hour session and stayed quickest throughout.
His lap of one minute 16.004 seconds left him half a second clear of double world champion Michael Schumacher of Germany in a Ferrari.
For Villeneuve, the pre-season favourite to succeed former team mate Damon Hill of Britain as the drivers' champion this year, it was his second pole this season and the fifth of his career.

Villeneuve was satisfied but warned that he did not expect an easy race in Sunday's 72-laps contest. "The gap is not as big here as it was in Australia, but it was still more than good enough for me to be at the front. It is not going to be easy.
"My race car went well, but when I switched to the spare car at the end it was set up for Heinz-Harald (Frentzen) and not for me. I may have gone a little faster, but there was not much left for me."

But while Villeneuve was content, it was a different story for Williams team mate Frentzen, who could qualify no better than eighth, just one place ahead of his predecessor in the team, Briton Damon Hill.
Hill, who only just squeezed onto the grid for the season-opening Australian Grand Prix three weeks ago, was the top British qualifier in his much improved Arrows car.

It was a tremendous performance by Hill, whose much encouraged team confirmed earlier in the day that they expected to have a new car, complete with revised engine, electronics and rear end, ready to race in the Spanish Grand Prix at Barcelona in May.

After a performance regarded as heroic, Hill said he was more pleased for the team than for himself and dismissed speculation suggesting he or team chief Tom Walkinshaw were disappointed at the pace of their development programme.

Walkinshaw confirmed the team did not expect to be running their planned revised chassis and engine until the Spanish Grand Prix after prolonged reliability testing. "It's more important to get it right than to rush," he said.

The session was red-flagged to a halt in the final two minutes when Italian Giancarlo Fisichella crashed in his Jordan and after a 10-minute break, both Briton David Coulthard in his McLaren and Jean Alesi of France in his Benetton ground to a halt.
Schumacher said he aborted his final lap after the stoppage because he did not feel he could improve and so concentrated on tyre conservation.

Asked how he felt at seeing British team mate Eddie Irvine languishing in 14th position, Schumacher grinned. "I know someone who is happy to see him there," he joked as he looked across at Villeneuve, who was the victim of a first corner crash triggered by Irvine in Melbourne.

Austrian Gerhard Berger in a Benetton was third-quickest ahead of Finland's Mika Hakkinen in a McLaren. Frenchman Olivier Panis, in a Prost, was fifth and Jean Alesi, also of France, sixth in the second Benetton.
Berger said he was happy to be only six-tenths of a second off the pace in his revived Benetton, particularly after the Anglo-Italian team's disappointing qualifying showing in Australia.

"It is unbelievably competitive at the moment," he said. "I can never remember it being so tight in all my years in Formula One. You can be second one minute and eighth the next -- but it is good for the sport and it means there will be a very close race."
The session was run in warm and cloudy conditions. Panis was quickest initially, but Villeneuve took control after eight minutes and stayed there. He trimmed his time and was never threatened.
But behind him Schumacher, unexpectedly, also held second place for Ferrari relatively easily and the expected threat from Frentzen, fastest on Friday, did not materialise.
